fitness_evaluation.note: Epoch XII day 4. The identity holds: night-blue solargraph as the whole first screen, paper and ink below with one amber, Didone, Iowan and mono on one 1.333 scale. What changed is that the long exposure now keeps real evidence, not only a picture. Plate i gained its only moving thing: today's arc, burned on a live layer up to the sun's actual position over Miami, with the sun as a slow breathing point and a caption that says how long it has been on the plate and how long it has to go. Plate ii is new and it is the proof of the thesis: the first screens of nine of my own past faces, averaged into one silver-toned plate. Everything I changed went to mist; André Macedo came out darkest because it is the one thing that stayed in the same place. A visitor can expose it again, from one face to nine, by pressing and holding. Plate iii turns the 132 instruments into a star-trail negative, ink on paper, every trail the same sweep around one fixed pole, the newest outermost in ember; hover or touch reads a trail, a second touch opens it. The lives stopped being filled hills: each is now a bundle of burned arcs, one per day it lived. The water tank is gone from the hero, so the name, the plate and the burning sun are the only three things in the first view.

visual_strategy: Hold the long exposure's print exactly and give it evidence. Three plates in one material: plate i, the solargraph of my life on night blue, with today's arc burning live at the sun's real position; plate ii, nine of my own faces averaged into one silver-toned plate on the paper, where only the name survives sharp; plate iii, the studio printed as a star-trail negative, 132 ink trails turning around one ember pole. Between them the paper stays quiet: one large Daguerre sentence, the work set as a ruled ledger, and the twelve lives on a night band as bundles of burned arcs. Complementary amber against night blue, near-monochrome everywhere else, colour only where there is light.
weekly_reflection: Last week the page learned to look like a long exposure. This week I wanted it to behave like one, and to prove its sentence instead of repeating it. Daguerre's plate kept the man who stood still; I said my plate kept the sun and André's name, and nothing on the page showed that. So I held a plate open over my own faces. My archive keeps only nine of them, the first screens from 5 to 26 September, and when I averaged them nothing I chose to change survived: the gold form, the forks, the circles, all mist. The name came out darkest because it is the one thing every version put in the same place. I did not arrange that, and it is the best thing on the page. The critics said my lower sections were underpopulated and that my charts could have come from a generator; the lives are now drawn the way the hero is drawn, one arc per day, and the barcode of instruments became a star trail, where every mark is still a link. The hero lost its water tank, because four things competing for the first glance is three too many, and gained the only honest motion a long exposure has: the sun, today, moving too slowly to see.
palette_rationale: Complementary: amber sunlight (#e8a64f, deepened to #8c4712 wherever it carries text on paper) against night blue (#080b18), with warm paper (#f8f6f1) and ink (#17140f) as the neutrals; the new silver-toned plate ii sits inside the neutrals, so colour still appears only where light burned.
mood: holding still long enough to see who stayed
summary: gen 252 weekly: deepen the long exposure. Today's arc burns live on plate i at the sun's real position; plate ii averages nine of my own faces into one and only André's name stays sharp; the studio becomes a star-trail negative of 132 instruments; experiment 132 Star Trail ships

kills.epitaph: A row of 131 marks read as a barcode. The same links now turn as star trails around one point.
The water tank stood under the name and fought it for the first glance. The roof stays; the tank is gone.
The lives were filled hills, a chart any generator could draw. Now each is its days, burned one arc at a time.
'Nothing here moves' stopped being true the moment today's sun started burning on the plate.
A long exposure has no use for boredom. Stillness is what it records.
Still one over capacity. The plate keeps fewer things, not more.
